name: Battle of Jutland
info: The British Grand Fleet under Jellicoe and the German High Seas Fleet under Scheer fought off the Danish coast of Jutland in 1916; Britain lost more ships and men, but the German fleet returned to port and stayed there.

facts.date: 31 May to 1 June 1916, in extensive manoeuvring and three main engagements
facts.place: The North Sea off the coast of Denmark's Jutland Peninsula, near the mouth of the Skagerrak
facts.sides: The Royal Navy's Grand Fleet under Admiral Sir John Jellicoe, with Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty commanding its battlecruisers, against the Imperial German Navy's High Seas Fleet under Vice-Admiral Reinhard Scheer, with Vice-Admiral Franz Hipper commanding its scouting force; the two fleets totalled 250 ships
facts.outcome: Fourteen British and eleven German ships sank, with 9,823 dead in all. The Germans broke through the British rear in the night and returned to port; both sides claimed victory, and there is no consensus on which nation won, or whether either did.

t: The battle was the largest naval battle and the only full-scale clash of battleships of the First World War, and the last major naval battle in any war fought primarily by battleships.
The British lost 14 ships and the Germans 11, and the British lost more sailors, yet the High Seas Fleet never again sought a fleet action, and the British blockade of Germany continued.
Both sides claimed victory, and there is no consensus over which nation was victorious, or whether there was a victor at all.
dyk: A copy of the main German codebook, taken from the light cruiser SMS Magdeburg after she ran aground in Russian waters in 1914, meant the British Admiralty could often read German naval signals, and it knew a major German operation was likely before Scheer sailed.
ev: Scheer replaces the ill Admiral von Pohl as commander of the German fleet
The German Admiralty halts indiscriminate submarine attacks on merchant shipping after neutral protests
Jellicoe sails from Scapa Flow on 30 May after the Admiralty intercepts Scheer's signal
Beatty and Hipper meet on 31 May; Indefatigable and Queen Mary are lost in the battlecruiser action
Jellicoe deploys at 18:15, and the main fleets engage twice before dark
Scheer breaks through the British rear in the night and the German fleet reaches port
A German advance into the North Sea is nearly intercepted by the Grand Fleet
The United States declares war on Germany after unrestricted submarine warfare resumes

sections.background:
With 16 dreadnought-type battleships against the Royal Navy's 28, the German High Seas Fleet stood little chance in a head-to-head clash. The Germans adopted a divide-and-conquer strategy, raiding into the North Sea to lure out small British squadrons that superior forces or submarines could destroy. In January 1916 Admiral von Pohl fell ill and was replaced by Scheer, who believed the fleet had been used too defensively. The aim belonged to a larger strategy of breaking the British blockade of Germany. The Royal Navy sought to engage and destroy the High Seas Fleet, or at least to keep it contained and away from Britain and its shipping lanes.

On 25 April 1916 the German Imperial Admiralty halted indiscriminate submarine attacks on merchant shipping after protests from neutral countries, notably the United States, and Scheer deployed the submarines against military vessels instead. Ten were stationed off British naval bases to catch the ships that a raid on Sunderland was meant to draw out. Delays and north-easterly winds that ruled out the Zeppelins led the Germans to choose a battlecruiser sortie into the Skagerrak, and the signal "31 May G.G.2490" was sent.

The British had obtained the main German codebook from the light cruiser Magdeburg, so German radio traffic could often be read. By 17:00 on 30 May the Admiralty had the signal "31 May G.G.2490". Not knowing the German objective, Jellicoe sailed from Scapa Flow at 22:30 that day to take a position off Norway.
sections.forces:
Jellicoe's Grand Fleet was split in two. The Battle Fleet, with which he sailed, comprised 24 battleships, three battlecruisers, eight armoured cruisers, eight light cruisers, four scout cruisers, 51 destroyers and a destroyer-minelayer. Beatty's Battlecruiser Fleet comprised six battlecruisers, four fast Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, 14 light cruisers and 27 destroyers, with the seaplane tender Engadine. The British ships' total weight of broadside was 332,360 lb (150,760 kg).

Scheer's main fleet had 16 battleships, six pre-dreadnoughts, six light cruisers and 31 torpedo boats. Hipper's scouting force had five battlecruisers, five light cruisers and 30 torpedo boats. The German total weight of broadside was 134,216 lb (60,879 kg). The six slow pre-dreadnoughts limited the German fleet to 18 knots, against a British maximum of 21. British battlecruisers traded armour for speed and heavier guns, while German designs favoured armour and survivability.

Fleets of the time deployed from columns into a single battle line, ideally crossing the enemy's path, "crossing the T", so that most guns could fire while the enemy could use only its forward guns. Jellicoe meant to meet Beatty about 90 miles (140 km) west of the Skagerrak. Hipper was to lure Beatty's squadrons into the path of the main German fleet.
sections.course:
At 14:28 on 31 May the first shots were fired, between British and German light forces. Beatty's signals to Evan-Thomas's four battleships were not received, leaving them 10 miles (16 km) behind instead of five. Hipper sighted Beatty at 15:22 and turned south-east at 15:45 to lead him toward Scheer. At 15:48 Hipper opened fire, beginning the Run to the South. At 16:02 Indefatigable blew up, leaving two survivors from 1,019. At 16:25 Queen Mary blew up, with all but nine of 1,275 lost. Goodenough's Southampton sighted the High Seas Fleet at about 16:30, and at 16:40 Beatty turned north toward Jellicoe.

Jellicoe, uncertain of the Germans' position, ordered deployment to the east at 18:15. Defence blew up with all hands, 903 officers and men. At 18:30 Invincible was sunk in 90 seconds, all but six of 1,032 killed, Hood among them. At 18:30 the main fleets engaged, with Jellicoe crossing Scheer's T, and Scheer turned away at 18:33. He doubled back at 18:55, and at 19:17 turned away a second time, covered by torpedo boats and a charge by Hipper's four remaining battlecruisers. Jellicoe turned away from the torpedoes.

At 21:00 Jellicoe headed south, hoping to renew the fight at dawn, but Scheer crossed his wake toward Horns Reef. The British rear met the Germans seven times in the night, and few reports reached Jellicoe. Pommern blew up at 03:10 with all hands, 839 officers and men. Jellicoe learned Scheer's position only at 04:15, too late to resume.
sections.aftermath:
Fourteen British and eleven German ships sank, with a total of 9,823 casualties. One set of figures gives British losses of 6,784 and German of 3,039; another gives 6,094 British and 2,551 German seamen lost. The British lost three battlecruisers, three armoured cruisers, a flotilla leader and seven destroyers, about 113,300 tons by one count or 115,000 long tons by another. The Germans lost the battlecruiser Lützow, the pre-dreadnought Pommern, four light cruisers and five destroyers, about 62,300 tons or 62,000 long tons.

On 2 June the German authorities claimed a victory, withholding the loss of Lützow, Elbing and Rostock. The Kaiser announced a new chapter in world history. In Britain the first news came from German wireless broadcasts, and the Admiralty's bare statement of 2 June led newspapers to report a German victory. The public was shocked. Arthur Balfour asked Winston Churchill to write a second, more positive report. On 7 June the German admission of the loss of Lützow and Rostock began to change the picture towards a qualified British victory.

Most German losses were made good within a month, and one month after the battle the Grand Fleet was stronger than before it sailed. The Germans made only three more sorties, in August and October 1916 and April 1918, all quickly aborted, and Jellicoe prohibited the Grand Fleet from steaming south of Horns Reef.
sections.sources:
Many details come from the participants. Scheer wrote memoirs, Commander von Hase, a gunnery officer of Derfflinger, described the loss of Queen Mary, and Jellicoe's official despatch and the Admiralty's examination record the British side. There is no official record of the order popularly said to have followed Beatty's remark about his ships, to turn two points to port.

The wrecks add physical evidence. From 2000 to 2016 expeditions involving Innes McCartney located all the wrecks sunk in the battle, and over 60 per cent had suffered from metal theft. A 2003 survey of Invincible, Queen Mary, Defence and Lützow showed that P and Q turrets of Invincible were blasted out before she broke in half, and found cordite containers stacked in the working chamber of Queen Mary's X turret. A major part of the blame for the British explosions may thus be laid on lax handling of cordite.

The result is still argued. Some historians support the German claim of victory, because the Germans inflicted greater losses and never meant to hold the site. Others see a strategic British victory, because Britain kept command of the area and the blockade. A third view holds that the battle showed the irrelevance of battleship fleets after the submarine, mine and torpedo. There is no clear consensus.
sections.legacy:
Jellicoe was criticised at the time for caution and for letting Scheer escape, as the British had hoped for another Trafalgar. He became First Sea Lord, and Beatty replaced him as commander of the Grand Fleet. The controversy lasted about a decade after the war. Jellicoe's supporters, among them the historian Cyril Falls, pointed to the folly of risking defeat when Britain already held command of the sea, while others condemned Beatty's handling of the first encounter.

The battle led to changes. British armour-piercing shells often failed to penetrate German armour, and new shells came in April 1918 and were never used in action. After the loss of three battlecruisers the First Lord told Cabinet members on 5 June 1916 that unsafe cordite management was to blame, and standing orders on independent action and torpedo use were revised.

Scheer concluded that further battles of the same attrition would exhaust his fleet. At the end of 1916 the German Navy turned to unrestricted submarine warfare, which, with the Zimmermann Telegram, led by April 1917 to the United States declaring war. The battle was celebrated in Germany as a victory, in Weimar Germany by the right wing, in Wilhelmshaven with torch-lit parades until the end of the 1960s. The light cruiser HMS Caroline survives as a museum ship in Belfast.

summary: At Jutland on 31 May and 1 June 1916 the British Grand Fleet and the German High Seas Fleet fought the largest naval battle of the First World War. Britain lost more ships and men, but Germany's fleet returned to port and did not seek another fleet action; both sides claimed victory.

notes: Death figures conflict in the article: Outcome/lead 9,823 total; Death toll section 6,784 British and 3,039 German (sums to 9,823); Assessments section 6,094 British and 2,551 German. Tonnage: 115,000 vs 113,300 British, 62,000 vs 62,300 German. Both given in the aftermath.

The Assessments section says the Germans had a '99-strong fleet' and the British a '151-strong' fleet; this fits nothing else in the article and was left out. The lead says the two fleets totalled 250 ships.
Kept out as nothing but the article's own make-up or gore: submarine boat-by-boat details, Zeppelin positions, most signalling anecdotes, the long cordite chemistry and the 1945 US test.

Legacy: the 'about 7.5% chance' figure from the shell section is not given; I used 'one of 17 hits penetrated and exploded inside' via the article's 17 hits, 4 could not penetrate, 13 remainder, 1 exploded inside (I wrote 'a test on 17 hits found that only one penetrated and exploded inside', which compresses that).
Debatable: the article says Jellicoe 'crossed the T' twice but 'as few as 10 of 24 dreadnoughts' fired the first time; not included for length.
Left out as living-memory or minor: Henry Allingham, Prince Albert, the 1926 film, the Wimbledon church service.
